title: Microprocessors & ARM Architecture
blurb: Microprocessor fundamentals, system components, memory hierarchy, performance, RISC, ARM architecture, registers, modes, CPSR, and endianness.
description: A university-aligned microprocessors and ARM architecture course built from the supplied EECE340 lecture material.

lessons.title: Microprocessor fundamentals & the CPU
objectives: Explain the CPU's role in a computer
lessons.explanation: A microprocessor is a computer's CPU implemented on a single integrated circuit. It fetches and executes instructions, performs arithmetic and logical work, and coordinates data movement with memory and I/O. Modern processors contain very large numbers of transistors connected to implement datapaths, control logic, caches, and other structures.
examples:
CPU on one chip
→ fetch instruction
→ decode instruction
→ execute operation
→ repeat
commonMistakes: Treating a microprocessor as the entire computer rather than the CPU that works with memory and I/O.
lessons.explain: A microprocessor is a computer's CPU implemented on a single integrated circuit. It fetches and executes instructions, performs arithmetic and logical work, and coordinates data movement with memory and I/O. Modern processors contain very large numbers of transistors connected to implement datapaths, control logic, caches, and other structures.

lessons.title: From early computers to modern microprocessors
objectives: Connect transistor scaling to processor capability
lessons.explanation: Processor development moved from large vacuum-tube systems to transistors, integrated circuits, and then complete CPUs on a chip. Integration reduced size and cost while allowing much larger transistor counts and more capable processors.
examples:
1940s: vacuum-tube computers
1947: transistor
1959: integrated circuit
1971: Intel 4004 commercial microprocessor
later generations: wider words, more transistors, more on-chip features
commonMistakes: Memorizing dates without understanding the architectural change each technology made possible.
lessons.explain: Processor development moved from large vacuum-tube systems to transistors, integrated circuits, and then complete CPUs on a chip. Integration reduced size and cost while allowing much larger transistor counts and more capable processors.

lessons.title: Computer components, microprocessors, microcontrollers & SoCs
objectives: Distinguish a microprocessor from a microcontroller
lessons.explanation: A computer system combines the processor with memory and I/O support. Cache keeps frequently needed data close to the CPU, DRAM provides larger working memory, and platform logic connects components and peripherals. A microcontroller integrates a CPU with memory and peripherals, while a system-on-chip integrates still more system functions.
examples:
General-purpose system: CPU ↔ cache ↔ main memory ↔ I/O
Microcontroller: CPU + memory + peripherals on one device
SoC: processor cores + memory/control blocks + many system functions
commonMistakes: Assuming microprocessors, microcontrollers, and SoCs differ only in speed rather than in integration and intended use.
lessons.explain: A computer system combines the processor with memory and I/O support. Cache keeps frequently needed data close to the CPU, DRAM provides larger working memory, and platform logic connects components and peripherals. A microcontroller integrates a CPU with memory and peripherals, while a system-on-chip integrates still more system functions.

lessons.title: Memory hierarchy & cache evolution
objectives: Describe the trend toward on-chip caches
lessons.explanation: Memory is organized as a hierarchy because no single technology is simultaneously the fastest, largest, and cheapest. Registers are closest to execution, then caches, then main memory. Processor history moved caches from the motherboard toward on-die L1, L2, and L3 levels.
commonMistakes: Thinking every memory access costs the same amount of time.
lessons.explain: Memory is organized as a hierarchy because no single technology is simultaneously the fastest, largest, and cheapest. Registers are closest to execution, then caches, then main memory. Processor history moved caches from the motherboard toward on-die L1, L2, and L3 levels.

lessons.title: Architecture vs microarchitecture
objectives: Explain how two processors can share an ISA
lessons.explanation: Architecture defines the programmer-visible contract, including instructions, registers, data types, and behavior. Microarchitecture is how a particular processor implements that contract. Two processors can execute the same instruction set while using different caches, pipelines, issue widths, or out-of-order machinery.
examples:
Architecture: what software can rely on
Microarchitecture: how the processor carries it out
Same ISA ≠ same internal design
commonMistakes: Using 'architecture' and 'microarchitecture' as interchangeable words.
lessons.explain: Architecture defines the programmer-visible contract, including instructions, registers, data types, and behavior. Microarchitecture is how a particular processor implements that contract. Two processors can execute the same instruction set while using different caches, pipelines, issue widths, or out-of-order machinery.

lessons.title: Processor performance: time, clock rate & IPC
objectives: Use execution time as the primary performance measure
Relate IPC/CPI and clock rate to performance
Explain why deeper pipelines have trade-offs
lessons.explanation: Processor performance is fundamentally about how long a workload takes. Clock frequency affects cycles per second, while IPC describes how much instruction work completes per cycle. Pipelining can raise frequency, dependencies and stalls reduce IPC, and superscalar or out-of-order execution can expose more parallel work.
examples:
instructions = 1_000_000
ipc = 2.0
clock_hz = 2_000_000_000
cycles = instructions / ipc
seconds = cycles / clock_hz
print(seconds)
commonMistakes: Assuming a higher clock rate automatically means a faster processor for every program.
lessons.explain: Processor performance is fundamentally about how long a workload takes. Clock frequency affects cycles per second, while IPC describes how much instruction work completes per cycle. Pipelining can raise frequency, dependencies and stalls reduce IPC, and superscalar or out-of-order execution can expose more parallel work.

lessons.title: RISC principles & ARM architecture
objectives: Connect ARM design choices to embedded systems
lessons.explanation: Classic RISC uses regular instructions, many registers, and explicit loads/stores for memory access. ARM data-processing instructions mainly use registers, while LDR and STR move data between registers and memory. A modern processor may be internally complex while preserving this programmer-visible architecture.
examples:
Memory → LDR → register
registers → ALU operation → register
register → STR → Memory
commonMistakes: Interpreting RISC as 'every real instruction always completes in exactly one physical clock cycle.'
lessons.explain: Classic RISC uses regular instructions, many registers, and explicit loads/stores for memory access. ARM data-processing instructions mainly use registers, while LDR and STR move data between registers and memory. A modern processor may be internally complex while preserving this programmer-visible architecture.

lessons.title: ARM data sizes, instruction sets & state
objectives: Distinguish ARM and Thumb instruction encodings
lessons.explanation: In the 32-bit ARM material, a halfword is 16 bits, a word is 32 bits, and a doubleword is 64 bits. Classic ARM instructions are 32 bits wide, while Thumb/Thumb-2 use a mixture of compact 16-bit and 32-bit encodings. Execution state controls which encodings the processor interprets.
commonMistakes: Confusing instruction encoding size with the size of the data being processed.
lessons.explain: In the 32-bit ARM material, a halfword is 16 bits, a word is 32 bits, and a doubleword is 64 bits. Classic ARM instructions are 32 bits wide, while Thumb/Thumb-2 use a mixture of compact 16-bit and 32-bit encodings. Execution state controls which encodings the processor interprets.

lessons.title: ARM programmer model & registers
objectives: Explain the roles of SP, LR, and PC
Explain why some modes use banked registers
lessons.explanation: Classic ARM exposes general-purpose registers plus special roles for R13 as stack pointer, R14 as link register, and R15 as program counter. CPSR records current status/control information. Privileged exception modes can access an SPSR and selected banked registers so handlers can preserve state and use their own stack/link context.
examples:
R0-R12 : general-purpose view
R13     : SP
R14     : LR
R15     : PC
CPSR    : current status/control
SPSR    : saved status in exception modes
commonMistakes: Assuming every processor mode sees exactly the same physical SP, LR, and saved-status registers.
lessons.explain: Classic ARM exposes general-purpose registers plus special roles for R13 as stack pointer, R14 as link register, and R15 as program counter. CPSR records current status/control information. Privileged exception modes can access an SPSR and selected banked registers so handlers can preserve state and use their own stack/link context.

lessons.title: Processor modes, CPSR, endianness & exception overview
objectives: Name the major classic ARM modes
lessons.explanation: Classic ARM has User mode and privileged modes including System, Supervisor, IRQ, FIQ, Abort, and Undefined. CPSR holds condition flags, execution state, interrupt masks, and mode bits. Little-endian stores the least-significant byte at the lower address; big-endian reverses that order. Exceptions enter an appropriate privileged mode so handlers can use protected state.
examples:
value = 0x12345678
print(value.to_bytes(4, "little").hex())
print(value.to_bytes(4, "big").hex())
commonMistakes: Reading the ARM I and F CPSR bits as interrupt-enable bits; in classic ARM, a set mask bit masks/disables that interrupt.
lessons.explain: Classic ARM has User mode and privileged modes including System, Supervisor, IRQ, FIQ, Abort, and Undefined. CPSR holds condition flags, execution state, interrupt masks, and mode bits. Little-endian stores the least-significant byte at the lower address; big-endian reverses that order. Exceptions enter an appropriate privileged mode so handlers can use protected state.

title: ARM Assembly Programming
blurb: ARM assembly syntax, data processing, barrel shifts, flags, condition codes, branches, memory addressing, stacks, functions, and exceptions.
description: A university-aligned ARM assembly course built from the supplied instruction, function, and exception lecture material.

lessons.title: ARM assembly structure, syntax & directives
lessons.explanation: ARM assembly source combines processor instructions with assembler directives. Most data-processing instructions place the destination first, followed by source operands. AREA, ENTRY, RN, EQU, ALIGN, SPACE, and END help the assembler organize code/data or define names; they are not operations executed by the CPU.
examples:
AREA Prog1, CODE, READONLY
        ENTRY
counter RN 0
limit   EQU 5
        MOV counter, #0
stop    B stop
        END
commonMistakes: Treating assembler directives such as AREA or EQU as instructions executed by the ARM core.
lessons.explain: ARM assembly source combines processor instructions with assembler directives. Most data-processing instructions place the destination first, followed by source operands. AREA, ENTRY, RN, EQU, ALIGN, SPACE, and END help the assembler organize code/data or define names; they are not operations executed by the CPU.

lessons.title: Registers, immediates, MOV & MVN
lessons.explanation: Data-processing instructions work primarily on registers. MOV copies an operand into a destination register, while MVN writes the bitwise complement. Immediate operands use # in the lecture syntax. Remember the destination-first pattern when tracing instructions.
examples:
MOV r0, #17
        MOV r1, r0
        MVN r2, r1
commonMistakes: Reading MOV r0, r1 as copying r0 into r1.
lessons.explain: Data-processing instructions work primarily on registers. MOV copies an operand into a destination register, while MVN writes the bitwise complement. Immediate operands use # in the lecture syntax. Remember the destination-first pattern when tracing instructions.

lessons.title: Arithmetic instructions: ADD, ADC, SUB, SBC, RSB & RSC
lessons.explanation: ARM arithmetic instructions typically use a destination and two input operands. ADD and SUB perform basic arithmetic; ADC and SBC include carry state for multiword arithmetic. RSB reverses subtraction order, useful when the desired calculation is operand2 minus operand1.
examples:
MOV r1, #9
        MOV r2, #4
        ADD r0, r1, r2
        SUB r3, r1, r2
        RSB r4, r1, r2
commonMistakes: Applying normal SUB operand order to RSB.
lessons.explain: ARM arithmetic instructions typically use a destination and two input operands. ADD and SUB perform basic arithmetic; ADC and SBC include carry state for multiword arithmetic. RSB reverses subtraction order, useful when the desired calculation is operand2 minus operand1.

lessons.title: Logical operations & bit manipulation
lessons.explanation: AND keeps bits selected by a mask, ORR sets selected bits, EOR performs XOR, and BIC clears bits selected by the second operand. These operations are central to packed flags and device/control registers.
examples:
MOV r0, #0x0F
        MOV r1, #0x03
        AND r2, r0, r1
        ORR r3, r0, #0x10
        EOR r4, r0, r1
        BIC r5, r0, #0x03
commonMistakes: Using arithmetic intuition for bit masks instead of tracing each bit position.
lessons.explain: AND keeps bits selected by a mask, ORR sets selected bits, EOR performs XOR, and BIC clears bits selected by the second operand. These operations are central to packed flags and device/control registers.

lessons.title: Barrel shifter: LSL, LSR, ASR & ROR
objectives: Combine a shift with a data-processing instruction
lessons.explanation: ARM can shift the second operand as part of many data-processing instructions. LSL shifts left, LSR shifts right with zero fill, ASR preserves the sign bit for signed values, and ROR rotates bits around. Combining ALU work with a shift is a characteristic ARM feature.
examples:
MOV r0, #7
        MOV r1, r0, LSL #1
        MOV r2, r1, LSR #2
        ADD r3, r0, r0, LSL #4
commonMistakes: Assuming LSR and ASR are identical for values whose top bit is 1.
lessons.explain: ARM can shift the second operand as part of many data-processing instructions. LSL shifts left, LSR shifts right with zero fill, ASR preserves the sign bit for signed values, and ROR rotates bits around. Combining ALU work with a shift is a characteristic ARM feature.

lessons.title: CPSR flags & the S suffix
objectives: Explain N, Z, C, and V
Use the S suffix to update flags
Separate signed overflow from unsigned carry
lessons.explanation: N reflects the result sign bit, Z indicates zero, C records carry/no-borrow information and shifted-out bits, and V reports signed arithmetic overflow. Many data-processing instructions update flags only when the S suffix is requested.
examples:
MOV  r0, #5
        SUBS r1, r0, #5
        MOVS r2, #-1
commonMistakes: Treating C and V as the same condition.
lessons.explain: N reflects the result sign bit, Z indicates zero, C records carry/no-borrow information and shifted-out bits, and V reports signed arithmetic overflow. Many data-processing instructions update flags only when the S suffix is requested.

lessons.title: CMP, CMN, TST, TEQ & conditional execution
objectives: Use comparison instructions to set flags
Choose a condition code from flag results
lessons.explanation: CMP behaves like subtraction for flag setting, CMN like addition, TST like bitwise AND, and TEQ like XOR. They update flags without keeping a normal destination result. Conditional suffixes such as EQ or NE make an instruction execute only when its flag condition is satisfied.
examples:
MOV r0, #2
        CMP r0, #2
        MOVEQ r1, #1
        MOVNE r1, #0
        TST r0, #2
commonMistakes: Expecting CMP to store a normal subtraction result.
lessons.explain: CMP behaves like subtraction for flag setting, CMN like addition, TST like bitwise AND, and TEQ like XOR. They update flags without keeping a normal destination result. Conditional suffixes such as EQ or NE make an instruction execute only when its flag condition is satisfied.

lessons.title: Branches, if/else & loops
lessons.explanation: Branch instructions change control flow by loading a new PC value. Labels identify targets. Conditional branches combine flag tests with control flow, which implements if/else and loops. Testing before or after the body distinguishes pre-test and post-test loops.
examples:
j       RN 0
        MOV j, #3
loop    CMP j, #0
        BLT done
        SUB j, j, #1
        B loop
done    B done
commonMistakes: Forgetting that a loop must modify the state used by its termination condition.
lessons.explain: Branch instructions change control flow by loading a new PC value. Labels identify targets. Conditional branches combine flag tests with control flow, which implements if/else and loops. Testing before or after the body distinguishes pre-test and post-test loops.

lessons.title: LDR/STR & ARM addressing modes
lessons.explanation: ARM is a load-store architecture, so memory values move into registers before most data processing. LDR/STR transfer words, with byte and halfword variants. Addressing modes combine a base register with an offset; pre-indexing forms the address before access, while post-indexing uses the base first and updates it afterward.
examples:
MOV r2, #0x1000
        MOV r0, #17
        STR r0, [r2]
        MOV r0, #23
        STR r0, [r2, #4]
        LDR r1, [r2]
        LDR r3, [r2, #4]
        STR r3, [r2, #8]
        LDR r4, [r2], #4
commonMistakes: Confusing the address in the base register with the data loaded from memory.
lessons.explain: ARM is a load-store architecture, so memory values move into registers before most data processing. LDR/STR transfer words, with byte and halfword variants. Addressing modes combine a base register with an offset; pre-indexing forms the address before access, while post-indexing uses the base first and updates it afterward.

lessons.title: LDM/STM, PUSH/POP & the runtime stack
lessons.explanation: LDM and STM move multiple registers between registers and memory. Addressing-mode suffixes specify increment/decrement and before/after behavior. PUSH and POP are stack-oriented aliases using R13/SP; in the convention shown in the lectures, PUSH corresponds to STMDB and POP to LDMIA, so the stack grows toward lower addresses.
commonMistakes: Assuming textual register-list order controls memory ordering.
lessons.explain: LDM and STM move multiple registers between registers and memory. Addressing-mode suffixes specify increment/decrement and before/after behavior. PUSH and POP are stack-oriented aliases using R13/SP; in the convention shown in the lectures, PUSH corresponds to STMDB and POP to LDMIA, so the stack grows toward lower addresses.

lessons.title: Subroutines, BL/BX LR & parameter passing
objectives: Call and return from a subroutine
Compare register, memory-block, and stack parameter passing
lessons.explanation: BL branches while saving a return address in LR/R14. A simple return can use BX LR. Subroutines preserve state according to the calling convention. Parameters can be passed in registers, through a referenced memory block, or on the stack; stack-based access must account for values pushed on entry.
examples:
main    MOV r0, #5
        BL double
        B stop

double  PUSH {r1}
        ADD r1, r0, r0
        MOV r0, r1
        POP {r1}
        BX lr
stop    B stop
commonMistakes: Calling another function without protecting LR when the current function still needs its own return address.
lessons.explain: BL branches while saving a return address in LR/R14. A simple return can use BX LR. Subroutines preserve state according to the calling convention. Parameters can be passed in registers, through a referenced memory block, or on the stack; stack-based access must account for values pushed on entry.

lessons.title: Exceptions, interrupts, vectors & SVC
objectives: List major classic ARM exception types
lessons.explanation: On a classic ARM exception, CPSR is copied to the relevant SPSR, the processor changes mode, a return address is stored in mode-specific LR, and PC goes to an exception vector. The vector dispatches to a handler, which returns using the exception-appropriate sequence. SVC deliberately requests a privileged OS service.
examples:
0x00  Reset
0x04  Undefined instruction
0x08  SVC
0x0C  Prefetch abort
0x10  Data abort
0x18  IRQ
0x1C  FIQ
commonMistakes: Using the same unadjusted LR return sequence for every exception type.
lessons.explain: On a classic ARM exception, CPSR is copied to the relevant SPSR, the processor changes mode, a return address is stored in mode-specific LR, and PC goes to an exception vector. The vector dispatches to a handler, which returns using the exception-appropriate sequence. SVC deliberately requests a privileged OS service.

quiz.q: AREA, ENTRY, EQU, and END are primarily:
quiz.explanation: AREA organizes a section, ENTRY marks an entry point, EQU defines a constant, and END ends the source. These direct the assembler rather than perform CPU calculations.

quiz.q: For a typical three-operand ARM data-processing instruction, the first register is usually:
quiz.explanation: In ADD r0, r1, r2, r0 receives the result while r1 and r2 supply values. Read the operands from destination to sources.
MOV r0, r1 reads r1 and writes its value into r0. r1 is unchanged.

options: The bitwise complement of its operand
quiz.explanation: MVN flips every bit of the source. In a 32-bit register, MVN applied to 0 gives 0xFFFFFFFF, not 1.
RSB reverses the usual SUB order: RSB r0, r1, r2 stores r2 minus r1 in r0.

options: A carry from a previous arithmetic step must be included
quiz.explanation: ADC computes operand1 + operand2 + C. This lets the carry from a low-word addition feed a high-word addition.
BIC computes operand1 AND NOT operand2. A 1 in the mask therefore clears the corresponding destination bit.
EOR sets a result bit when the two corresponding input bits differ; equal bits produce 0.

quiz.q: ASR differs from LSR because ASR:
options: Preserves the sign bit when shifting right
quiz.explanation: ASR replicates the top/sign bit while shifting right. LSR shifts zeros into the high positions.

options: Shift an operand as part of another data-processing instruction
quiz.explanation: ADD r0, r1, r2, LSL #2 shifts r2 left by two before adding it to r1. The shifted value need not be stored in a separate register.

quiz.q: The Z flag is set when the relevant result is:
quiz.explanation: Z is 1 when the flag-setting operation produces zero. A plain instruction without S usually leaves these flags unchanged.
V indicates that the mathematical signed result cannot fit in a signed 32-bit value. It is different from unsigned carry C.

options: Updates condition flags based on a subtraction-like comparison
quiz.explanation: CMP uses a subtraction to set NZCV but discards the arithmetic result. It does not overwrite either compared register.

quiz.q: TST primarily uses which logical operation for flag testing?
quiz.explanation: TST calculates a bitwise AND for the flags without saving that AND result in a destination register.

options: Condition flags and a condition code
quiz.explanation: The condition suffix reads flags set earlier. BEQ tests Z=1; BLT tests N different from V for a signed comparison.

quiz.q: A do-while style loop differs from a while loop because its body:
quiz.explanation: A do-while style loop places its test after the body, so the body runs at least once. A while style loop can skip the body when its first test fails.

options: Load data from memory into a register
quiz.explanation: LDR reads the word at an effective memory address and places it in the destination register. STR transfers a register value in the opposite direction.

options: Uses the current base address, then updates the base
Updates the base before the access only
quiz.explanation: LDR r0, [r1], #4 loads using the old address in r1, then increases r1 by four. The offset is outside the brackets.
PUSH preserves register values in memory on the stack and adjusts SP. It is useful before a subroutine changes values the caller needs.

quiz.q: In the stack convention shown in the lectures, the stack grows toward:
quiz.explanation: In the full descending convention, reserving stack space decreases SP; releasing it increases SP. Lower memory addresses hold newer stack entries.

quiz.q: BL does what in addition to branching?
options: Saves a return address in LR
quiz.explanation: BL saves the address of the instruction after the call in LR before transferring control. A nested call must preserve a needed earlier LR.

quiz.q: A simple subroutine commonly returns with:
quiz.explanation: BX LR branches to the saved return address. LR must still hold the intended return address for this to work.

quiz.q: On classic ARM exception entry, CPSR is copied into:
quiz.explanation: Classic ARM exception entry saves the old CPSR in the target mode SPSR so the handler can later restore the interrupted status. The tracer does not model exception entry.

options: Request a privileged software service by raising a software exception
quiz.explanation: SVC deliberately raises a software exception to request a supervisor service. It is not an ordinary BL subroutine call; handling depends on the execution environment.
